abstract: "Journals increasingly require authors to share data and code, but checking whether submitted articles comply is effortful. Cooper and the BES Data and Code Hackathon Group (2026) manually coded data- and code-archiving practices in 1861 papers published in the seven British Ecological Society journals between 2017 and 2024, in a two-day hackathon with 145 participants. We examine to what extent this information can be extracted automatically from an article and its linked repositories. We used Metacheck, an open source tool that checks articles and repositories for best practices, to assess the same articles and compared the results with the manual coding. Agreement was 86% on whether data were available in a repository, 88% on whether code was archived, 96% on whether the data had a licence, and 73% on whether a README was present; where both found data or code, agreement on whether it could be downloaded was above 99%. We used an LLM (Claude Opus 5.5) to assist in reviewing every disagreement. About two in five of the papers where coders found data or code that Metacheck missed had not shared it in a way a machine can retrieve; most other disagreements reflect technical limitations of Metacheck, such as imperfect text extraction from PDF files or lack of support for a minority of repositories or file types. For READMEs, most disagreements reflect a difference in what counts as a README. The manual coding was not always right: for licences, the automated coding was correct in 46 of 57 disagreements. We also used Metacheck to run the code of 435 papers: 22% of 2874 scripts ran without an error, revealing common problems authors can resolve. Automated tools can find data and code that human coders miss, and could substantially reduce the time needed for such checks. While they cannot replace human judgement, automated tools can support workflows that check whether data and code are shared following FAIR principles."

# Introduction

The last two decades have seen a notable culture change around open science practices. Universities, journals, and funders increasingly expect researchers to engage in open science practices. One open science practice that has become especially widely required is data and code sharing. The goal of data and code sharing is to facilitate re-use, and to increase transparency. Many funders have started to require data management plans that specify where and how data and code will be made available for re-use, and submission guidelines for journals often require that data and code underlying the claims in a manuscript are shared if possible. The British Ecological Society, for example, requires, "as a condition for publication, that all data supporting the results in papers published in its journals are archived in an appropriate public archive offering open access and guaranteed preservation", and for theoretical papers that "the underlying model code must be archived" (<https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/hub/data_archiving_policy>).

Although the requirements to share data and code are clear, checking whether authors follow through on them is difficult. At the BES journals, for example, journal staff check each accepted paper to ensure that data and code are archived, but "do not have the skills or capacity to guarantee" requirements such as completeness [@cooper2026, p. 1955]. Manually checking data and code files is a time-consuming task that requires expertise about best practices in data and code sharing. Cooper and the BES Data and Code Hackathon Group [-@cooper2026] assessed data- and code-archiving practices across the seven journals published by the British Ecological Society (BES). They found that most manuscripts in which data was used also shared the data, but code sharing was less common, and even when data and code were shared, best practices were often not followed. About a third of repositories lacked a README file, and code was not always well-annotated. Studies in other fields show that data and code are often not shared, even when journals require it [@hamilton_how_2022; @li_formalistic_2026], and that when code is shared, rerunning it often fails or does not reproduce the reported results [@trisovic_largescale_2022; @obels2020; @cruwell_whats_2023; @miske_investigating_2026]. These findings strongly suggest that it would be beneficial if data and code are reviewed before a manuscript is published.

Some journals manually check data and code before an article is published. This practice is well established in economics journals, where a dedicated Data Editor oversees the reproduction of results based on data and code [@vilhuber_report_2025]. Manual checks are laborious and delay the publication process. It is therefore not surprising that researchers are exploring automated ways to check whether data and code are shared, and whether they are usable. For example, the Scalable Infrastructure for Validation of Computational Social Science Research (SIVACOR), a project led by the Data Editor of the American Economic Association, examines whether it is possible to automatically verify the computational reproducibility of data and code. The extent to which automated processes can reduce the workload associated with checks of data and code sharing practices is an open question. Automation has the potential to reduce the workload of manual checks, but it is not clear whether and where automated tools can achieve the same level of accuracy as human coders.

```{r}
#| label: cooper-summary
n_coded <- as.numeric(table(master_comparison$recorder_ID))
n_coders <- length(n_coded)
n_papers <- sum(n_coded)
median_per_coder <- median(n_coded)
min_per_coder <- min(n_coded)
max_per_coder <- max(n_coded)
```

In this paper we will examine how Metacheck, a novel open source tool that checks best practices in research reporting, including data and code sharing, might assist in the process of checking whether data and code are shared. We will compare the output of Metacheck against the manual coding of Cooper et al. [-@cooper2026], available at <https://github.com/nhcooper123/reproduce-reuse-recycle>, which we treat as a careful human comparison rather than as a ground truth that is correct by definition. It is clear that the human coders exerted considerable effort over the 2-day hackathon to code the `r n_papers` papers, where `r n_coders` people coded a median of `r median_per_coder` (min = `r min_per_coder`, max = `r max_per_coder`) manuscripts. Cooper et al.'s protocol covered the seven journals published by the British Ecological Society (BES), coding papers published between 2017 and 2024 on eight groups of questions per paper. The team coded whether data and code were used and archived, where they were archived, whether the archived files could be located, downloaded, and opened, what file formats were used, whether a README was present and how useful it was, how complete the archived data were, how well-annotated the code was, and whether the data and code were citable (i.e., had a DOI and a licence).

Coding the presence or absence of data and/or code files is exactly the kind of time-consuming task that automated tools such as Metacheck [@R-metacheck] aim to support. If an automated tool could complete some of Cooper et al.'s eight coding questions at comparable accuracy to human coders, it would substantially reduce the workload that is currently required to check if researchers follow best practices in data and code sharing. Metacheck [@R-metacheck] is a modular, open-source tool that uses text search, rule-based classification, APIs, and optional large language models to extract information about research practices from scientific manuscripts and their associated repositories. Metacheck's `repo_check`, `data_check`, and `code_check` modules perform automated checks that closely resemble the classifications that Cooper et al. [-@cooper2026] asked their human coders to perform.

In this paper, we use Cooper et al.'s openly archived data as the comparison coding [@cooper2026zenodo], and for each of the eight groups of questions in their protocol, we summarize what Cooper et al. found, and examine whether that question can currently be automated with sufficient accuracy. Where the two codings disagree, we used Claude Opus 5.5 to assist reviewing each case to see which is correct, rather than assuming the human coding is right by definition. The results generated by Metacheck are completely automated, do not rely on AI, and can be reproduced by re-running the code. Human input was limited to a few settings, which are recorded in the code: two papers whose repositories hold large archives were given a larger download limit than the 2000 MB used for all other papers, and for one paper, whose repository holds 23 GB of data, the files were listed but not downloaded. Re-running the code also requires access keys for the APIs of GitHub, Dryad, OSF, and Zenodo. Unlike a validation study that reports a single accuracy percentage, our goal here is to make transparent where the current version of Metacheck can reduce the manual burden of this kind of meta-scientific data collection, and where it cannot.

Automated tools perform most reliably on data and code being shared according to the FAIR principles, the idea being that "all research objects should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) both for machines and for people" [@wilkinson_fair_2016, p. 3]. Human coders can retrieve information that is not accessible by a machine. For example, if authors share their data as a table in a PDF file in the supplementary material, the data are not FAIR: a table in a PDF cannot be read reliably by a machine, and the file has no persistent identifier of its own. Cooper and colleagues did not limit their coding to FAIR data, and as a consequence, Metacheck will always miss some information that human coders found. On the other hand, machines can find some information that human coders miss. For example, Metacheck found information about licenses, READMEs, and repositories that human coders failed to classify. Throughout this project we will also reflect on practical challenges when developing software that attempts to automatically retrieve FAIR data, and the implications for best practices in data and code sharing.

# Methods

We obtained the list of paper DOIs, journals, and years from the cleaned dataset in the public repository, after correcting four DOIs that were wrong in that dataset, and downloaded the articles from the publisher and from Europe PMC with an R script; the full texts are not shared because of copyright. All articles were converted to structured text using GROBID 0.9.0, and converted to Metacheck paper objects. We ran the `repo_check` (locates and lists files in online repositories), `data_check` (classifies files and extracts information about tabular data), and `code_check` (checks R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB code files) modules to mirror the manual coding performed by Cooper and colleagues. Subsequently, we ran the `reproducibility_check` module to illustrate additional benefits of automation.

## 1. Does the paper use data/code? If so, are they archived?

Cooper and colleagues reported that "Of the 1861 papers in our dataset, 93% (n = 1735) used data and 90% (n = 1670) used code. Of these papers, 97% (n = 1690) archived their data, but only 35% (n = 577) archived their code". The first two percentages are based on text in data availability statements and the method section. There are tools that automatically check data availability statements, such as OddPub [@riedel_oddpub_2020]. Metacheck itself has an equivalent module, `open_practices`, which reads the full text and judges from the wording alone whether open data and/or open code was shared. These automated checks most closely follow the coding by Cooper and colleagues, in that data and code is classified as available irrespective of whether authors followed FAIR principles. Metacheck's `repo_check` module takes a different approach and classifies data and code as available based on a linked repository that can be automatically accessed through an API.

### Oddpub and Open Practices Check

OddPub [@riedel_oddpub_2020] is a tool that searches text for keywords related to data and code sharing. The Metacheck Open Practices module does the same, but is intentionally over-inclusive, which means it is designed to find more data or code sharing statements, while also returning more false positives. We compared the automatic text-based judgements from OddPub and the Open Practices module to Cooper and colleagues' human coding of whether data and code were openly shared (their `data_open`/`code_open` columns), treating "Yes" (and for data "Yes, but not all files") as open and "No" as not open, and excluding papers where the coders used an ambiguous label (e.g., "Needs specific software or too large") or left the item unscored (`data_open`/`code_open` were only asked for papers Cooper and colleagues had already coded as archiving their data/code, and not every such paper has a recorded answer, so the denominators below are smaller than the archiving counts reported earlier). As with the comparison above, this is a comparison against the human coding by Cooper and colleagues, not against a known correct answer, so a disagreement means only that the tool and the human coders reached different judgements. 

For data sharing (`r opdata$n` papers with a clear human judgement), OddPub agreed with the human coders on `r pct1(opdata$accuracy)` of the papers (`r opdata$n_disagree` disagreements: `r opdata$n_tool_open_cooper_not` where OddPub judged the data open but the coders did not, and `r opdata$n_tool_not_cooper_open` the other way around). Metacheck's `open_practices` module agreed with the human coders on `r pct1(mcdata$accuracy)` of the papers (`r mcdata$n_disagree` disagreements: `r mcdata$n_tool_open_cooper_not` where `open_practices` judged the data open but the coders did not, and `r mcdata$n_tool_not_cooper_open` the other way around). For code sharing (`r opcode$n` papers with a clear human judgement), the gap was larger: OddPub agreed `r pct1(opcode$accuracy)` of the time (`r opcode$n_disagree` disagreements: `r opcode$n_tool_open_cooper_not` and `r opcode$n_tool_not_cooper_open`), whereas `open_practices` agreed `r pct1(mccode$accuracy)` of the time (`r mccode$n_disagree` disagreements: `r mccode$n_tool_open_cooper_not` and `r mccode$n_tool_not_cooper_open`). The disagreements fall almost entirely on one side: both tools much more often judge a paper to share open data or code than the human coders judge it not to, and this corpus contains very few papers the human coders judged as clearly *not* sharing (`r opdata$n_negative` for data, `r opcode$n_negative` for code), so the counts of papers the tools agreed were not open rest on very small numbers. `open_practices` and OddPub both determine open data/code from the text of the article alone, but do not examine whether data and code are shared by examining the contents of data repositories, as other Metacheck modules do.

Note that OddPub and `open_practices` classify every paper regardless of how Cooper and colleagues' coders scored this question. For data sharing, `r n_blank_data_open` papers archived their data (`data_availability == "Yes"`) but were left unscored on whether it could be opened, of which OddPub judged `r npcnt(n_oddpub_open_blank_data, n_blank_data_open)` and `open_practices` judged `r npcnt(n_mc_open_blank_data, n_blank_data_open)`) to have open data; a further `r n_ambig_data_open` were explicitly flagged by Cooper and colleagues' coders as needing specific software or too large to open, of which OddPub judged `r npcnt(n_oddpub_open_ambig_data, n_ambig_data_open)` and `open_practices` judged `r npcnt(n_mc_open_ambig_data, n_ambig_data_open)` to have open data. For code sharing, `r n_blank_code_open` papers archived their code (`code_archived == "Yes"`) but were left unscored on whether it could be opened, of which OddPub judged `r npcnt(n_oddpub_open_blank_code, n_blank_code_open)` and `open_practices` judged `r npcnt(n_mc_open_blank_code, n_blank_code_open)` to have open code; a further `r n_ambig_code_open` were explicitly flagged as possibly accessible with the right software, of which OddPub judged `r npcnt(n_oddpub_open_ambig_code, n_ambig_code_open)` and `open_practices` judged `r npcnt(n_mc_open_ambig_code, n_ambig_code_open)` to have open code.

### Repo check, Data check, and Code check

Cooper and colleagues found that `r n_cooper_data` papers archived their data and `r n_cooper_code` their code, and in total, `r n_cooper_either` papers archived either data or code. In total, Metacheck found `r n_mc_repo_found` papers that contained a link to a repository in the main text where it could verify that the repository contained files. Of these, `r n_mc_data` papers contained data, `r n_mc_code` papers contained code, and `r n_mc_either` papers contained either data or code according to the Metacheck modules that examine the data and code in repositories. The manually coded classifications agree with the automatic classification by Metacheck for `r n_both_yes_either` papers, and disagree for `r n_either_total_disagree` (`r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` where Cooper's coders found data or code that Metacheck missed, and `r n_mc_yes_cooper_no` papers where Metacheck found data or code that Cooper's coders had not coded as shared).

For Metacheck, data and code is findable and accessible if it is archived in one of the repositories that Metacheck supports (through its support for Dataverse, DSpace 6 and 7, Figshare, and DataOne, and dedicated support for OSF, Zenodo, ResearchBox, Dryad, ReShare, GitHub, GitLab, Mendeley Data, FSD, AsPredicted, and 4TU). Because many repositories use the same underlying API, Metacheck supports `r n_unique_repos` unique repositories (`r n_dataverse_hosts` Dataverse installations, `r n_dspace7_hosts` DSpace 7 installations, `r n_dspace_legacy_hosts` legacy DSpace 6 installations, `r n_dataone_hosts` DataOne member nodes, and `r n_figshare_hosts` Figshare-based hosts, plus `r n_dedicated_platforms` dedicated single-platform integrations), but this is only a subset of all repositories used in manuscripts.

```{r}
#| label: full-317-audit-load

source("code/full_audit.R")
```

We used Claude Opus 5.5 to assist in reviewing the `r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` papers where Cooper and colleagues' coders coded data or code as shared and where Metacheck failed to find data or code. This review was done one paper at a time by checking the contents of the repository and revealed five reasons Metacheck misses data and code in a repository (see @tbl-audit-reasons). In `r n_no_repo_cited` papers we found no reference to a repository or link to a dataset in the manuscript. The data were either explicitly withheld for confidentiality, ethical, or Indigenous-data-sovereignty reasons, could not be shared for legal reasons, or were in shared in the paper or its supplemental material. Some of these papers offer to make data available upon request, but are arguably better classified as papers that explain why data could not be shared. In `r n_nonfair` papers the citation or the repository did not meet basic FAIR requirements, so the data could not be retrieved automatically when we checked. Papers cite a private reviewer or share link instead of the dataset's public identifier (`r n_nonfair_private_link` papers), or an organisation or user page that identifies no specific deposit (`r n_nonfair_no_deposit`); or the repository blocks automated access (`r n_nonfair_blocked`), was not live or accessible when checked (`r n_not_live`), or offers no API through which a machine can retrieve the data (`r n_unsupported_not_fair + n_nonfair_no_api`). Automated access to repositories has become harder in recent years because of heavy scraping of files, which repository managers assume is mostly done by bots collecting training data for generative AI. In a 2025 survey of 66 repositories, over 90% reported aggressive bot traffic, often causing slowdowns or outages, and many responded with rate limits and other blocks that also stop legitimate machine access [@shearer2025aibots]. We observed this directly when attempting to download files for this manuscript.

In `r n_unsupported_but_fair` papers, data is shared on a repository that is FAIR, but Metacheck does not yet support automated downloads from this repository. Metacheck does not yet have support for some field-specific or institutional repositories (for example, the US Geological Survey's ScienceBase, the Environmental Data Initiative, the NERC Environmental Information Data Centre, and PANGAEA, the earth- and environmental-science data publisher). We found `r n_not_classified` papers that shared data or code in a repository Metacheck supports, but in a format Metacheck is not able to automatically classify as data or code. This occurred when data was shared in non-FAIR formats (e.g., a table in a PDF file), or data or code files in a plain .txt file without labeling the file as data or code (which makes it difficult to automatically differentiate them from output or documentation files in a repository, while a human can find such data). Another reason was that the file extension is not in the list of files that metacheck classifies as data. For example, drone photographs that are the measurement data in JPG files are classified as image material rather than data by Metacheck. Finally, archives in `.rar` or `.7z` formats can't be opened by R, and Metacheck can not (yet) examine their contents.

For the remaining `r n_metacheck_limitation` papers, the repository is FAIR and on a platform Metacheck supports, but a technical limitation prevented Metacheck from finding or using it. In `r n_lim_extraction` papers, the PDF to text conversion corrupted the repository identifier, most often by inserting spaces into a DOI (`r n_lim_doi_garbled` papers), or the text produced by GROBID lacked the data availability statement, usually because this section followed the reference list (`r n_lim_text_missing`). 

The remaining `r n_lim_code` papers reflect limitations of Metacheck's own code. In `r n_lim_ref_only` of these papers, the DOI of the repository appeared only in the reference list, which Metacheck does not search. In `r n_lim_ref_citation` papers the authors referred to their data only through a data citation; in the other `r n_lim_ref_conversion` the authors did give the DOI in the data availability statement, but the conversion from PDF to text moved it into the reference list or scrambled the statement. Data citations allow assigning credit to the reuse of data, and are therefore good practice, but it is difficult for a machine to identify which DOIs in a reference list point to the data underlying the manuscript. We therefore strongly recommend to always also provide a direct link to the DOI of the repository holding the authors' own data in the main text, for example in a data availability statement. In the remaining `r n_lim_code - n_lim_ref_only` papers Metacheck did not follow a Handle link to a repository it supports (4 papers), did not recognise the identifier (a Figshare collection or institutional DOI, 3 papers; an Arctic Data Center identifier that is not a DOI, 1 paper), or did not read files inside an archive (2 papers). The full per-paper record for every one of these `r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` papers is available in `data/review/manual_repo_findability_audit_data.csv` and `data/review/manual_fair_api_findability_audit_data.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-audit-reasons
#| tbl-cap: "Reasons and frequencies of papers where manual coders found data or code while Metacheck did not."

full_audit_summary_table <- data.frame(
  Cluster = c(
    "No repository is cited anywhere in the paper's own text",
    "Repository contains data or code that Metacheck did not classify (a format Metacheck does not yet support, or data or code not shared in a FAIR format)",
    "Citation or repository is not FAIR (a private or non-specific link, a repository that blocks automated access or is not live, or a platform without an API)",
    "Repository is FAIR, but on a platform Metacheck does not support",
    "Technical limitation: the repository is FAIR and on a supported platform, but the PDF-to-text conversion or a defect in Metacheck's own code prevented detection or classification"
  ),
  `n papers` = c(n_no_repo_cited, n_not_classified, n_nonfair, n_unsupported_but_fair, n_metacheck_limitation),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Tables are plain Markdown tables (knitr::kable), which Quarto writes as real Typst
# tables and apaquarto formats in APA style; flextable has no Typst output.
knitr::kable(full_audit_summary_table, format = "pipe", align = c("l", "r"))
```

In total, `r n_no_repo_cited` papers did not link to a repository, `r n_not_fair_format` of the `r n_not_classified` papers whose files Metacheck did not classify shared their data or code in a format that is not FAIR, and `r n_nonfair` papers linked to a repository, or used a link, that is not FAIR. This means that `r n_not_fair_total` of the `r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` papers where Cooper and colleagues' coders found data or code that Metacheck missed are explained by data and code that were not shared following FAIR principles. In other words, of the `r n_cooper_either` papers that Cooper and colleagues' coders coded as sharing data or code, the remaining `r n_cooper_fair` shared them in a way that allows an automated tool, in principle, to locate the repository and access the files, and Metacheck found the data or code in `r n_both_yes_either` of these, or `r pct_fair_found`. Resolving technical limitations in text extraction from PDF files, and support for additional repositories would resolve the remaining discrepancies.

## 2. Where were the data/code archived?

Cooper and colleagues coded the specific repository where data and/or code was stored. They note that 60% of the code files hosted on GitHub or similar platforms were also archived on Zenodo [@cooper2026, p. 1959]. GitHub is not a stable repository, as owners can change or delete files, while Zenodo is. Cooper et al. report Dryad as the dominant data repository in the papers they examined (57%, n = 1022), with Figshare (9%), Zenodo (12%), and "various institutional and government repositories" (17%) making up most of the remainder [@cooper2026, p. 1959].

<!--
Double-checking, does metacheck list presence of data/code files for *each* repo in a paper separately, or for the aggregate of all repos? As previously written, below sounded like the latter, but I think is the former, so I revised it.
-->

Cooper and colleagues separately coded the repository that stored the data and the repository that stored the code, and both data and code can be stored in more than one platform per paper. Metacheck does not distinguish between data and code repositories, but lists whether each repository it finds contain data and/or code files. We retrieved the repository address from Metacheck and assigned each repository to the categories used by Cooper and colleagues (the categories "Supplementary materials" and "Personal website" are not used by Metacheck, as it is designed to only find FAIR repositories). We then classify agreement into five categories: both name the same platforms, Metacheck names fewer platforms, Metacheck names more platforms, each names a platform the other does not, or they share no platform.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-archive-platform
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement between Cooper et al.'s coded archive platform(s) and the platform(s) of the repositories in which Metacheck found data or code, compared as sets of platforms."
# tbl-colwidths: [9, 12, 15, 15, 15, 20, 14]

platform_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("data_archive", "code_archive"), function(k) {
  r <- results[[k]]
  ct <- r$categories
  n <- r$n_both_coded
  f <- function(x) sprintf("%d (%.2g%%)", x, 100 * x / n)
  data.frame(
    Platform = if (k == "data_archive") "Data" else "Code",
    `Comparable papers` = n,
    `Same platforms` = f(ct[["exact"]]),
    `Metacheck lists fewer` = f(ct[["mc_fewer"]]),
    `Metacheck lists more` = f(ct[["mc_more"]]),
    `Each lists one the other lacks` = f(ct[["partial"]]),
    `No shared platform` = f(ct[["none"]]),
    check.names = FALSE)
})) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = 3:7, names_to = "Comparison") |>
  mutate(name = sprintf("%s (n = %s)", Platform, `Comparable papers`)) |> 
  select(-Platform, -`Comparable papers`) |>
  pivot_wider()
knitr::kable(platform_table, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 2)))
```

For data, `r results$data_archive$n_both_coded` papers could be compared because human coders and Metacheck named at least one repository platform. The two sides named exactly the same platform(s) for `r results$data_archive$n_agree` (`r pct1(results$data_archive$pct_agree/100)`) and agreed on at least one shared platform for `r results$data_archive$n_any_overlap` (`r pct1(results$data_archive$pct_any_overlap/100)`). Some of the differences are caused by the previously discussed limitations in the repositories that Metacheck supports, but other times Metacheck found more repositories than human coders. In `r results$data_archive$categories[["mc_fewer"]]` papers Metacheck lists fewer platforms than the coders, most often missing a second repository coded as "Other repo/database" (e.g., an institutional or domain-specific database). In `r results$data_archive$categories[["mc_more"]]` papers Metacheck found an additional platform holding data-classified files that the human coders missed, most often GitHub (`r n_data_mc_more_github` papers). Usually this is the authors' own repository holding data files alongside the analysis code, but in `r tp$n_data_archive_mc_more_to_exact` papers it is a repository of software the authors used, written by someone else.

Metacheck cannot yet differentiate between data or code that authors created and shared, and data or code that they reused, and it treats all files in repositories linked to in a manuscript as the paper's own data or code. Cooper and colleagues asked coders to count data the paper generated or collated, but did not record whether archived files were created by the authors. We asked Claude to examine each of the `r tp$n_github_repos` links to GitHub and GitLab that Metacheck found, and it judged that `r tp$n_third_party_repos` of these links, in `r tp$n_third_party_papers` papers, point to a repository whose owner is not an author of the manuscript or their research group. With one exception these hold software or scripts the authors used, not reused data; the exception is the repository of a text corpus, linked to by `r tp$n_corpus_papers` papers. Authors can make re-use of data or code created by others more transparent and automatically detectable by only using data citations for such repositories. There should not be a direct link to a repository that is re-used in the main text.

## 3. Can the archived data/code be located, downloaded and opened?

Cooper et al. report that, of the 1735 papers in their dataset that used data, 1690 archived the data, of which 97% could be accessed via the links provided in the data availability statement, 95% could be downloaded, and 91% could be opened [@cooper2026, p. 1959]. Cooper et al.'s coders downloaded data for `r n_dl_cooper_yes` papers; for `r n_dl_mc_na` of these papers Metacheck downloaded no data file at all, mostly because it did not find the repository (because the data were not shared in a FAIR way, were in a FAIR repository Metacheck does not support, or because of the technical limitations discussed earlier). Counted over all `r n_dl_cooper_yes`, Metacheck downloaded and could use the data in `r n_dl_mc_true` papers (`r pct1(n_dl_mc_true / n_dl_cooper_yes)`). For the `r results$data_download$n_both_coded` papers where both Metacheck and the manual coders gave an answer, they agreed for `r results$data_download$n_agree` (`r pct1(results$data_download$pct_agree/100)`), and in `r results$data_download$n_disagree` papers there was a disagreement.

We resolved each of the `r results$data_download$n_disagree` disagreements by downloading and opening the files. For `r vt(verdict_tallies$data_download, "COOPER_RIGHT")` the manual coders were correct. In `r n_dl_right("(?i)separated by spaces|space-separated")` the data are space-separated tables, which Metacheck cannot read, and `r n_dl_right("max_file_size")` of these also exceeds its 100 MB download limit. In `r n_dl_right("GeoTIFF")` the data are GeoTIFF and shapefile files inside a zip archive. In `r n_dl_right("Sequence Read Archive|NCBI SRA")` the data are in NCBI's Sequence Read Archive, a FAIR repository Metacheck does not support. In `r vt(verdict_tallies$data_download, "METACHECK_RIGHT")` the review judged Metacheck's answer correct, but this needs care, because Metacheck's answer combines two conditions: the files can be downloaded, and they contain a usable data table. In three papers the data were Excel files with formatted publication tables rather than raw data, and in a fourth the files are model-input files for Stan rather than raw data. In these four papers the files download, as the coders recorded, but they are not usable data tables, which is what Metacheck's answer requires. In the other two the coders' answer was wrong. One is an OSF project that the manual coder reported needing to request access to, although OSF's activity log shows it has been public since January 2021. The other linked to an Excel file for which the manual coder reported a download error, but that Metacheck downloaded without problem.

With respect to code sharing, Cooper et al. report that "only 35% (n = 577) archived their code" among papers using code [@cooper2026, p. 1958], and, among archived code, that most is on Zenodo or GitHub-family platforms [@cooper2026, p. 1959]. Cooper et al.'s coders and Metacheck both gave an answer on whether code was archived for `r results$code_archived$n_both_coded` papers. They agreed on `r results$code_archived$n_agree` (`r pct1(results$code_archived$pct_agree/100)`) and disagreed on `r results$code_archived$n_disagree` (`r pct1(1-results$code_archived$pct_agree/100)`). Concerning the question whether shared code could be downloaded, for `r results$code_download$n_both_coded` papers (which is the subset of papers where code was archived) there was almost perfect agreement between manual and automatic classifications (`r results$code_download$n_agree` of `r results$code_download$n_both_coded` (`r pct1(results$code_download$pct_agree/100)`), with only `r results$code_download$n_disagree` disagreement remaining).

We investigated all `r nrow(code_categories)` disagreements about whether whether code was archived (and the one disagreement about whether code could be downloaded). The manual coders were correct in `r vt(verdict_tallies$code_archived, "COOPER_RIGHT")` papers and Metacheck was correct in `r n_code("coders_wrong")` papers, and in `r vt(verdict_tallies$code_archived, "BOTH_WRONG")` papers both were wrong. In `r n_code("not_fair")` papers the code was not shared following FAIR principles. Metacheck could not find the code, but manual coders could. Out of these `r n_code("not_fair")` papers, in `r n_code_reason("only the Dryad page links")` authors shared data on Dryad and code on Zenodo, but the paper never directly linked to the Zenodo repository. Instead, the link to Zenodo was only present inside the Dryad repository. Authors should link to code directly in the data availability statement, using the Zenodo DOI. In `r n_code_reason("only in journal Supporting Information")` papers the code is provided only as journal Supporting Information, in `r n_code_reason("saved as .txt")` it is saved as a `.txt` file or without a file extension, in `r n_code_reason("link to a GitHub account")` the paper links to a generic GitHub account of an authors, instead of the specific GitHub repository that contains the shared files, and in `r n_code_reason("Word or PDF")` the code is inside a Word or PDF document. In the remaining `r n_code_reason("named only by the coders") + n_code_reason("no longer exists") + n_code_reason("private share link")` papers the paper gives no link to the code, a private share link, or a GitHub repository that no longer exists.

In the remaining `r n_code("metacheck")` papers the cause lies in earlier mentioned technical limitations of Metacheck, and the manual coders were correct in `r vt(verdict_tallies$code_archived, "COOPER_RIGHT") - n_code("not_fair")` of them. In `r n_code_reason("repository named in the paper not found")` papers Metacheck did not detect the repository named in the paper, in `r n_code_reason("platform Metacheck does not support")` the code is in a FAIR repository on a platform Metacheck does not support, in `r n_code_reason("written by other people")` Metacheck counted software or scripts written by other people as the authors' code, in `r n_code_reason("language or file type")` the code is in a language or file type Metacheck's `code_check` module does not cover, and in `r n_code_reason("archive Metacheck does not open")` it is inside an archive Metacheck does not open. In the remaining `r n_code_reason("README in R Markdown") + n_code_reason("R-package rule")` papers Metacheck counted a README written in R Markdown as code, or incorrectly classified data and code shared as an R package as software, instead of as the data and code of the paper. In `r vt(verdict_tallies$code_archived, "BOTH_WRONG")` of these `r n_code("metacheck")` papers both sides were wrong. The authors' code is on Zenodo and is linked only from the Dryad page, so the coders' answer that no code was archived is incorrect. Metacheck did not find this code, and its answer that code was archived is a false positive, because it rests only on a file called `README.Rmd`: in one paper in the Dryad deposit, in the other in a repository of another author's R package.

Third, in `r n_code("coders_wrong")` papers the manual coding was incorrect, and Metacheck's answer was correct. In `r n_code_reason("coders coded no code")` papers the coders coded that no code was archived, although the authors' code is in the repository. In one of these the repository holds the first author's general solver for the model the paper applies, in the folder of a companion paper, although the paper does not say that it used these scripts. In `r n_code_reason("coders coded code as archived")` papers the coders coded code as archived, but we found none. In the remaining paper, which is the one disagreement about downloading code, the coder reported that the link to the code and data did not open. The DOI in the paper leads to an OSF project that has been public since January 2022, before the coding took place, and Metacheck downloaded its R files without problem.

## 4. What file extensions do the archived data/code files use?

```{r}
#| label: file-extension-counts

# File extensions of the files Metacheck recognises as data and code, counted as
# Cooper et al. count them: each extension once per paper, with related extensions
# grouped, here also the files that belong to a shapefile.
group_extension <- function(x) {
  x[x %in% c("csv", "tsv")] <- "csv/.tsv"
  x[x %in% c("doc", "docx")] <- "doc(x)"
  x[x %in% c("xls", "xlsx")] <- "xls(x)"
  x[x %in% c("rda", "rdata", "rds")] <- "rda/.rdata/.rds"
  x[x %in% c("shp", "shx", "dbf", "prj", "cpg", "sbn", "sbx")] <- "shp"
  x
}
data_files <- structure_slim[structure_slim$data_type %in% "data", ]
data_files$ext <- tolower(tools::file_ext(data_files$file_name))
data_files <- data_files[nzchar(data_files$ext), ]
n_data_ext_raw <- length(unique(data_files$ext))
data_files$ext <- group_extension(data_files$ext)
data_ext <- unique(data_files[, c("paper_id", "ext")])
data_ext_counts <- sort(table(data_ext$ext), decreasing = TRUE)
n_data_ext <- nrow(data_ext)
n_data_ext_top10 <- sum(data_ext_counts[1:10])
data_ext_top10 <- paste0(".", names(data_ext_counts)[1:10], collapse = ", ")

code_files <- code_table_slim
code_files$ext <- tolower(tools::file_ext(code_files$file_name))
code_ext <- unique(code_files[, c("paper_id", "ext")])
n_code_ext <- nrow(code_ext)
n_code_ext_notebook <- sum(code_ext$ext %in% c("rmd", "qmd", "ipynb"))
n_code_ext_native <- n_code_ext - n_code_ext_notebook
code_languages <- unique(code_files[, c("paper_id", "language")])
n_code_languages <- nrow(code_languages)
n_code_language_r <- sum(code_languages$language %in% "R")
```

Metacheck can only report the extensions of files it recognises as data or code, so these numbers are not directly comparable to those of Cooper et al. [-@cooper2026, p. 1960]. Files recognised as data were archived with `r n_data_ext_raw` different file extensions, and of the `r n_data_ext` unique data file extensions recorded per paper, `r pct1(n_data_ext_top10 / n_data_ext)` (n = `r n_data_ext_top10`) were saved with the following 10 file extensions: `r data_ext_top10`. Of the `r n_code_ext` unique code file extensions recorded per paper, `r pct1(n_code_ext_native / n_code_ext)` (n = `r n_code_ext_native`) were saved as native source code, and a further `r pct1(n_code_ext_notebook / n_code_ext)` (n = `r n_code_ext_notebook`) as notebook files. Most code in FAIR formats that Metacheck could detect (`r pct1(n_code_language_r / n_code_languages)`, n = `r n_code_language_r`) was written in R.

## 5. Do the archived data/code have a README (or equivalent)? If so, how useful is it?

```{r}
#| label: readme-counts

# Metacheck has one README signal per paper, so Cooper et al.'s two questions are
# collapsed in the same way for the comparison in the text.
n_mc_readme <- sum(side_by_side$mc_any_readme %in% TRUE)
n_cooper_readme <- sum(side_by_side$cooper_any_readme %in% TRUE)
stopifnot(all(side_by_side$mc_data_availability[side_by_side$mc_any_readme %in% TRUE]))

# Papers that count only through the code question, and the papers without a README
# file whose deposit has a description or abstract on a Dryad web page.
readme_answers <- c("Yes", "Quasi-README")
n_cooper_readme_data <- sum(side_by_side$data_README %in% readme_answers)
n_cooper_readme_code_only <- sum(side_by_side$code_README %in% readme_answers &
                                   !side_by_side$data_README %in% readme_answers)
stopifnot(n_cooper_readme_data + n_cooper_readme_code_only == n_cooper_readme)
n_readme_description_dryad <- sum(readme_cooper_yes & review$any_readme_verdict %in% "DIFFERENT_DEFINITION" &
                                    grepl("landing page|description|abstract", review$any_readme_comment, ignore.case = TRUE) &
                                    grepl("dryad", review$any_readme_comment, ignore.case = TRUE))
```

Cooper et al.'s coders were asked whether the data had a "README/metadata", and a README or equivalent was present for 66% (n = 1114) of papers that shared data, and 61% (n = 351) of the papers that shared code [@cooper2026, p. 1960]. In total, `r pct1(n_cooper_readme / n_cooper_either)` of papers with either data or code included information equivalent to a README. Metacheck checks whether a repository contains a README file, which it determines from the file name (e.g., 'README' or 'data description' in various ways this can be written), or a RO-Crate metadata file. We do not report README quality, because how useful a README is requires a judgement only humans can make. Metacheck found a README file for `r npcnt(n_mc_readme, n_mc_repo_found)` of the `r n_mc_repo_found` papers with a repository that contains files, which is substantially lower than the manual coders found. The largest cause of disagreement is what counts as a README for Metacheck, compared with the manual coders. In `r vt(verdict_tallies$any_readme, "DIFFERENT_DEFINITION")` papers the coders recorded a README or equivalent, but the deposit holds no README file. For `r n_readme_description` of these the deposit's web page has a description or abstract, `r n_readme_description_dryad` of them on Dryad, and the coders may have counted this as the equivalent of a README (there are no details on what coders counted). We recommend that researchers add a README file to every repository (and preferably a RO-Crate file), as information on websites is typically not accessible through an API, and therefore not FAIR.

## 6. How complete is the archived data, and can the code be run?

```{r}
#| label: reproducibility-counts

source("code/reproducibility_counts.R")
```

Cooper et al. asked coders to judge how complete the archived data were, but note that "Completeness is difficult to assess thoroughly without reproducing the analyses in the paper, but this requires time and advanced computational skills" [@cooper2026, p. 1957]. They report that 69% (n = 1087) of datasets were scored as complete, and that "this should be considered an informed judgement about completeness, not verified reproducibility" [@cooper2026, p. 1960]. Metacheck has code that attempts to automatically reproduce results from data and code in R and Python. We ran the code in a Docker environment that contained the most common pre-installed packages, although this might lead to a difference between the code used to create the script, and the code used to run the script. We set a runtime for each script of at most 3000 seconds, and noted when scripts failed because they needed a longer time to run (e.g., lengthy simulations). When a script reads the output of another script, the module tries to run them in the required order. It changes the code to remove obstacles that are unrelated to the analysis: in `r n_rc_changed_papers` papers it rewrote `r n_rc_change("path_rewrite")` file paths so that they pointed to the downloaded files, removed `r n_rc_change("setwd_removed")` `setwd()` calls, added `r n_rc_change("library_injected")` calls that load a package, and replaced `r n_rc_change("font_replaced")` references to fonts. The results below therefore describe what happens after these repairs, and code run exactly as shared would fail more often. Finally, the module extracts the statistical results printed by the code, and looks for the statistics reported in the paper among them. This is a feature still under development, but it attempts to indicate which statistical tests can be found in the results of the reproduced code.

Of the `r n_mc_code` papers in which Metacheck found code, the module tried to run the code of `r n_rc_papers`. The other `r n_rc_not_run` papers only have MATLAB or Mplus code, which the reproducibility check module can't run, as this is proprietary software. Not every code file in these papers is a standalone analysis that the module runs on its own, so these files are counted and reported separately rather than among the scripts that were run: `r n_rc_source` files are run by another script through `source()` or an import and have no result of their own, `r n_rc_defines` only define functions, `r n_rc_jags` are JAGS or BUGS model files, `r n_rc_not_r_content` are not code in a language the module runs, and `r n_rc_not_downloaded` could not be tried because a data file they read was larger than the 1,000 MB per-file limit, and the datafile was not downloaded. Across these `r n_rc_papers` papers, `r n_rc_scripts` scripts were run as analyses, of which `r npcnt(n_rc_ok, n_rc_scripts)` ran without an error (`r n_rc_r_ok` of the `r n_rc_r` R scripts (`r pct1(n_rc_r_ok / n_rc_r)`) and `r n_rc_python_ok` of the `r n_rc_python` Python scripts (`r pct1(n_rc_python_ok / n_rc_python)`)). At the level of papers, all scripts ran without an error in only `r n_rc_all_ok` papers (`r pct1(n_rc_all_ok / n_rc_papers)`), some files ran in `r n_rc_some_ok` (`r pct1(n_rc_some_ok / n_rc_papers)`), and none of the files ran in `r n_rc_none_ok` (`r pct1(n_rc_none_ok / n_rc_papers)`).

@tbl-repro-reasons sorts the `r n_rc_failed` scripts that failed, in `r n_rc_failed_papers` papers, by the one-word reason the module saved for each script. A paper can appear under several reasons. The module did not start `r n_rc_outcome("dependency_unavailable")` scripts because a package they need could not be installed, and a further `r n_rc_outcome("not_parsed")` files could not be read as code. The other scripts started and then stopped: `r n_rc_outcome("errored")` with an error, `r n_rc_outcome("timed_out") + n_rc_outcome("skipped_time_limit")` on the time limit, `r n_rc_outcome("needs_a_person")` because the code asks a person to choose a file, `r n_rc_outcome("out_of_memory")` on the memory limit, `r n_rc_outcome("download_too_large")` because a download they need was too large, and `r n_rc_outcome("needs_internet")` because they need the internet.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-repro-reasons
#| tbl-cap: "Reasons why scripts did not run without an error. A paper can appear under several reasons."

knitr::kable(rc_reason_table, format = "pipe", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

The most frequent reason is a file the script needs. This can mean that the authors did not archive it (sometimes because the data could not be shared for privacy reasons), that it is produced by a step that is not archived, or that Metacheck could not match the name in the code to a file in the repository (as people sometimes rename files they share after they have run the analyses). In a further `r n_reason("interactive")` scripts the code asks a person to select a file, for example with `file.choose()`, so it cannot run unattended. The next most frequent reason, after `r n_reason("other")` scripts that stopped with some other error while the code ran, is a package. The papers declared `r n_rc_declared` packages in total, and `r n_rc_not_installed` of these (`r pct1(n_rc_not_installed / n_rc_declared)`) could not be installed, in `r n_rc_not_installed_papers` papers. In `r n_rc_not_on_cran` cases the package was not available on CRAN for the version of R the module used. The packages that failed most often are `r names(rc_failed_packages)[1]` (`r rc_failed_packages[[1]]` papers), `r names(rc_failed_packages)[2]` (`r rc_failed_packages[[2]]`) and `r names(rc_failed_packages)[3]` (`r rc_failed_packages[[3]]`). Some failures do not concern the authors' analysis at all, because Metacheck treats all files in a linked repository as the paper's own.

These results can be compared with the coders' judgement of completeness. Among the `r n_rc_complete` papers whose code was run and whose data the coders rated as complete, the module could not find a file a script needs in `r n_rc_complete_missing` papers (`r pct1(n_rc_complete_missing / n_rc_complete)`), compared with `r n_rc_missing_all` of all `r n_rc_papers` papers (`r pct1(n_rc_missing_all / n_rc_papers)`). At least one script ran without an error in `r n_rc_complete_any_ok` of these papers (`r pct1(n_rc_complete_any_ok / n_rc_complete)`), and all scripts did in `r npcnt(n_rc_complete_all_ok, n_rc_complete)`. The completeness ratio is not a valid indication of the computational reproducibility of a paper, Cooper et al. already caution.

This automated computational reproducibility check indicates that creating computationally reproducible data and code is difficult. Running a tool such as Metacheck on a repository before depositing data and code would perhaps have warned the researchers who failed to share all files that some scripts or files were missing, that objects or functions were not defined, or that there were other errors in the code. To prevent problems with packages or dependencies that are no longer available, the best solution is to create a Docker capsule which stores all required software, data, and code to reproduce the analyses. This is the only way to guarantee that scripts can be run years from now. Better coding practices would prevent researchers from creating code that requires human input, or where file paths are not set correctly. Finally, we could perhaps have increased the percentage of successful reproductions by increasing the run-time, and the file size of downloaded files. However, some limits should be set, and ideally scripts are computationally reproducible without downloading very large files, or running code for hours. Although the computational reproducibility rates might have been higher if a human had attempted to reproduce the results, the human coder would - for example - need expertise in python and R, the knowledge how to re-organize repositories, resolve minor coding errors, know which undefined libraries to install, and be able to figure out the order in which files should be run. Most researchers have not received training in computational reproducibility, and our results show there is a lot to gain. Automated checks such as those provided by Metacheck can reduce common errors, but real long term computational reproducibility might require alternative solutions than just sharing data and code, such as sharing all files in a container that guarantees computational reproducibility. \[We should do this ourselves and link to it\]

## 7. How good is the code annotation?

```{r}
#| label: code-annotation-counts

# Comment lines per code file, from code_check. A file Metacheck could read is flagged
# when none of its lines are comments, which is the module's own warning. A Python file
# without `#` comments is reported separately when it holds a docstring instead.
targets::tar_load(res_code_check, store = "_targets")
cc_files <- res_code_check$table[!is.na(res_code_check$table$percentage_comment), ]
n_cc_files <- nrow(cc_files)
n_cc_papers <- length(unique(cc_files$paper_id))
cc_zero <- cc_files$percentage_comment == 0
n_cc_zero <- sum(cc_zero)
n_cc_zero_papers <- length(unique(cc_files$paper_id[cc_zero]))
cc_zero_py <- cc_zero & cc_files$language %in% "Python"
n_cc_zero_py <- sum(cc_zero_py)
n_cc_zero_py_docstring <- sum(cc_files$has_docstring[cc_zero_py] %in% TRUE)
cc_comment_median <- median(cc_files$comment_lines)
cc_comment_q <- quantile(cc_files$comment_lines, c(.25, .75), names = FALSE)
cc_code_median <- median(cc_files$code_lines)

# Cooper et al.'s rating of annotation, from 1 (not annotated at all) to 10 (thorough
# annotation throughout). rc_cooper is read in the chunk reproducibility-counts above.
cc_rating <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(rc_cooper$code_annotation_scale))
n_cc_rated <- sum(!is.na(cc_rating))
cc_rating_median <- median(cc_rating, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Cooper et al.'s coders rated how well the code was annotated, on a scale from 1 (not annotated at all) to 10 (thorough annotation throughout) [@cooper2026, p. 1957]. For the `r n_cc_rated` papers they rated, the median score was `r cc_rating_median` [@cooper2026, p. 1960], although the authors note that this variable was less consistent among coders and should be interpreted with care [@cooper2026, p. 1958]. How good code annotation is cannot be classified automatically: whether a comment explains a decision that is not obvious from the code, or only repeats what the code does, requires a judgement that only human coders can make. Metacheck can check whether code is annotated at all. It counts the comment lines in every code file it can read, and warns when a file has no comments. Of the `r n_cc_files` code files in `r n_cc_papers` papers that Metacheck could check, `r npcnt(n_cc_zero,n_cc_files)`, in `r n_cc_zero_papers` papers, had no comments. Of these, `r n_cc_zero_py` were Python files, `r n_cc_zero_py_docstring` of which were documented with a docstring instead of comments, which Metacheck reports separately. The median code file had `r cc_comment_median` comment lines (interquartile range `r cc_comment_q[1]` to `r cc_comment_q[2]`), against `r cc_code_median` lines of code. Metacheck can not evaluate annotation quality, but it can warn when code is not annotated at

## 8. Are the data/code citable?

Cooper et al. report that "of the 1690 papers with archived data, 91% (n = 1543) had a DOI and 85% (n = 1438) had a licence", with CC0, the licence used by Dryad, used most often (n = 1076), and that "of the 577 papers with archived code, 79% (n = 457) had a DOI and 74% (n = 428) had a licence", with CC BY (n = 122), the licence Zenodo uses by default, and CC0 (n = 104) used most often [@cooper2026, p. 1960]. Metacheck reads the licence from the metadata of each repository it can access, and we compared whether the data had a licence. For the `r results$data_license$n_both_coded` papers where both the manual coders and Metacheck gave an answer, they agreed for `r results$data_license$n_agree` papers (`r pct1(results$data_license$pct_agree/100)`) and disagreed for `r results$data_license$n_disagree` (@tbl-summary). In `r results$data_license$fp` of these disagreements Metacheck found a licence that the coders did not record, and the review of each disagreement judged the automatic coding correct in `r vt(verdict_tallies$data_license, "METACHECK_RIGHT")` of the `r results$data_license$n_disagree`. We did not compare DOIs or the licences of code.

# Discussion

Researchers should share data and code following FAIR principles where possible. Manually checking whether data and code is shared correctly is time-consuming. We explored the extent to which automated tools can identify whether data and code is shared, and if best practices (e.g., including a README) are adopted. If automated tools can perform this task accurately, the workload for editors or peer reviewers who want to check whether submissions follow open science principles can be reduced substantially.

@tbl-summary summarizes how well Metacheck, a module based open source tool that can check data and code repositories for best practices, can identify data and code, the presence of a README and license, compared to the manual classifications of a team of 145 participants of a hackathon. The results show that in a substantial percentage of papers an automated check is able to identify the presence of downloadable data and code in a repository. Metacheck agrees with the classifications by manual coders for more than 85% of data and code repositories. In some of the disagreements, Metacheck can correctly identify data and code that manual coders missed. Other disagreements are due to the fact that Metacheck is designed to only identify FAIR data and code, while manual coders also classified non-FAIR repositories, and due to technical limitations of Metacheck (e.g., imperfect extraction of text from PDF files, unsupported repositories, imperfect processing of some data and code file-types).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 6, 7, 14, 11, 11, 11, 11, 9]
#| tbl-cap: "Agreements and disagreements between manual and automatic coding of data and code sharing practices."

# results already loaded in the data chunk above.
# Shorter labels for the table only; the full labels (results$label) are used
# in the prose. This also sets which constructs appear, and their order; the
# data_archive/code_archive platform-set rows are left out here on purpose.
short_label <- c(
  data_availability = "Data availability",
  data_license      = "Data licence present",
  data_download     = "Data downloadable and usable",
  code_archived     = "Code archived",
  code_download     = "Code downloadable",
  any_readme        = "Any README present"
)
# Each disagreement has exactly one review verdict, so these five categories
# sum to the disagreement count for every construct.
tally <- function(nm, verdict) if (!is.null(verdict_tallies[[nm]]))
  sum(verdict_tallies[[nm]][names(verdict_tallies[[nm]]) == verdict]) else 0L
summary_rows <- lapply(names(short_label), function(nm) {
  r <- results[[nm]]
  data.frame(
    Construct = unname(short_label[nm]),
    n = r$n_both_coded,
    `Agree %` = round(r$pct_agree, 1),
    Disagreements = r$n_disagree,
    `Manual coding correct` = tally(nm, "COOPER_RIGHT"),
    `Automatic coding correct` = tally(nm, "METACHECK_RIGHT"),
    `Different definition` = tally(nm, "DIFFERENT_DEFINITION"),
    `Both defensible` = tally(nm, "BOTH_DEFENSIBLE"),
    `Both wrong` = tally(nm, "BOTH_WRONG"),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
})
summary_tbl <- do.call(rbind, summary_rows)

# The first column is left-aligned and the numbers right-aligned; Typst wraps
# the long headers within their columns.
knitr::kable(summary_tbl, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 8)), row.names = FALSE)
```

The current results indicate that Metacheck can assist in the classification of data and code, especially when data and code is shared following FAIR principles. When Metacheck can't find data or code, it might still be shared, and in the 15% of cases where Metacheck missed data or code, manual coding remains necessary. Furthermore, Metacheck is currently unable to distinguish a GitHub link to a repository that shared the authors' code from a link to existing software that was used by the authors. Manual checks will remain necessary, and Metacheck is designed to assist, not replace human judgment. Despite several imperfections in the current version of Metacheck, we hope it can substantially reduce the time that scientists need to check whether articles share data and code.

Future research could improve both how Metacheck works, as how people share data and code. First, PDF files are created to optimize human readability, not machine readability. Text extraction from PDF files has known limitations which lead to broken or undetected links to repositories. It might be possible to remedy this by developing software that improved text extraction from PDF files [e.g., bibr, @werner_bibr_2026], but a fully machine-readable solution would require authors or publishers to share the machine readable XML files used to generate manuscripts, or to add metadata files alongside journal publications with important information (such as links to data and code). Second, automated tools should eventually support all FAIR repositories. Given the diversity of data and code storage solutions across disciplines, this will require collaboration between tool builders, research communities, and data repository managers. Third, automated tools should detect all file formats that store data and code, which once again given the diversity of research software used across disciplines requires collaboration between tool builders and research communities.

The comparison against the manually coded papers also highlights aspects where researchers, journals, and repositories can improve. Researchers should follow best practices in machine readable FAIR data and code sharing [@lakens_best_2026], and journals should ask authors to follow FAIR principles. Automated tools such as Metacheck can assist in such checks, as the current manuscript demonstrates. Repositories should be FAIR, and accessible by a machine. The Dryad repository does not allow downloads of file contents without an API key, and Dryad has stricter limits on the number of API calls, which severely limits automated checks. Researchers are recommended to share data in fully machine accessible repositories, such as Zenodo, instead.

The manually coded data be Cooper et al. [-@cooper2026] was extremely valuable to improve Metacheck. Over the course of preparing this manuscript we carefully compared the automated results of Metacheck against the manually coded results by Cooper and colleagues. This led us build in support for the backends of data repositories (e.g., Dataverse, DSpace, DataOne, and Figshare) where we previously supported only specific instances of data repositories, raising support from 6 data repositories to over 250. Numerous changes and improvements were made to Metacheck to allow it to support a wider range of data and code formats, and deal better with the the way researchers currently share datasets. For this reason, we believe projects where the scientific literature is systematically coded across different disciplines for features that researchers in these communities deem valuable will continue to be extremely important to develop tools like Metacheck. Appendix A documents in full detail how Metacheck improved over the course of this project.

It is essential that tools can automatically retrieve the data and code underlying scientific manuscripts to achieve the full potential these research outputs. Metacheck offers researchers and journals an easy way to check if data and code are shared and follow FAIR principles. As open science practices increase the demands on researchers, automated tools can assist and reduce the burden, while increasing the quality and value of scientific research.
